For oscillatory Gaussian perturbations, this overlap is the coherent sum of the positive- and negative-frequency branches of the source, with its amplitude factorizing exactly into a Gaussian spectral envelope and an interference factor. We observe that the excitation amplitude peaks at $ν=ω_n^{\rm Re}$ only for narrowband sources. For sufficiently broadband pulses, the maximum lies at $ν=0$, so efficient excitation does not necessarily require matching the carrier and the mode frequency. We observe that the interference between branches, modulates the amplitude only for nonzero $ν$, a feature generic to real oscillatory sources. The prominence of the interference-induced modulation is controlled by the ratio $ω_n^{\rm Re}/ω_n^{\rm Im}$. The phase separates into a mode-only, a width-only and a $ν$-dependent term, the last generated by the same interference, with $ν=0$ being its unique maximum at fixed width. The analytical predictions are validated against time-domain numerical simulations, showing a relative median error of $\sim 4\%$ for $|C_0|$. For $|C_1|$, the median error is $\sim 16\%$ when $σ\leq 5$, increasing to $\sim 36\%$ across the full parameter space. The median phase difference for $n=0$ is $\sim0.14 \,\rm rad $ and for $n=1$, $σ\leq5$ it is $0.34\,\rm rad$. Our results demonstrate that QNM excitation cannot be understood through frequency matching alone and may provide qualitative insights into more realistic astrophysical scenarios.

papers.title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
papers.authors: Zhaoying Pan; Yipei Wang; Shenyu Lu; Xiaoqian Wang
papers.abstract: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.

papers.title: Grasping the Future: Joint 3D Hand-Object Forecasting From Internet Videos
papers.authors: Rustin Soraki; Matthew Wallingford; Ryan Aby; Brandon Chee; Jason Ren et al.
papers.abstract: To interact with an object, we need to anticipate both how it will move and how our hands should move with it. Human videos capture these relationships across everyday activities, offering a natural source for learning to predict future interactions. Learning from them requires recovering motion from completed interactions and using it to anticipate what could happen next. We present $\textit{Grasping-the-Future}$, a unified generative model of joint 3D hand-object motion, including wrist motion, finger articulation, and object position and orientation. Through masked spatiotemporal completion and flow matching, we train a single model for several prediction tasks: forecasting future interactions, predicting hand motion given object motion or vice versa, generating both trajectories toward a desired final object pose, and completing partially observed interactions. We explicitly model hand-object relations and incorporate contact constraints to help preserve grasp relationships during motion. To obtain 3D supervision from internet videos, we develop a scalable pipeline that combines pretrained perception models with joint geometric optimization to reconstruct completed interactions. We combine these recovered trajectories with annotated interaction datasets as training data for all tasks. We demonstrate strong performance across all tasks, outperforming released forecasters on datasets with 3D annotations. Moreover, we show geometric and physical plausibility of the predicted trajectories by retargeting them to a robotic embodiment. Videos are available at https://grasping-the-future.github.io.

papers.title: Click3R: Interactive Stereo 3D Reconstruction with Sparse Correspondence Clicks
papers.authors: Hao Gu; Jin Yao; Zezhou Cheng
papers.abstract: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.

papers.title: Optimal Injectivity of the SparseStack
papers.authors: Lorenzo Beretta; Simone Bombari; Margalit Glasgow; Raphael Arkady Meyer; Kijun Shin et al.
papers.abstract: An Oblivious Subspace Injection (OSI) is a random sketching matrix that reliably preserves the minimum singular value of any fixed subspace with high constant probability, requiring only a one-sided spectral lower bound without controlling upper singular values. While classical Oblivious Subspace Embeddings (OSEs) fundamentally require row sparsity $Ω(\log r)$ at linear sketch dimension $k = O(r)$, we show that one-sided injectivity permits strictly sparser sketches, establishing matching (up to $\log\log r$ factors) upper and lower bounds of $\tildeΘ(\sqrt{\log r})$.   First, we prove that the SparseStack sketch achieves constant injectivity at linear dimension $k = Θ(r)$ with row sparsity only $ζ= O(\sqrt{\log r})$, well below the $Θ(\log r)$ barrier where standard operator-norm concentration fails. Second, we establish a matching lower bound: any isotropic random sketching matrix satisfying a mild row-overlap condition requires row sparsity $ζ= Ω(\sqrt{\log r / \log \log r})$ to achieve linear-dimension injectivity, confirming that the $\sqrt{\log r}$ scale is fundamental.   To bypass the lack of an operator-norm upper bound when $ζ= O(\sqrt{\log r})$, we decouple the sketch into two independent halves and introduce three techniques: (i) a uniform lower bound for flat vectors via randomized rounding, controlling discretization error using solely the Frobenius norm; (ii) a Gaussian truncation and minimax duality argument showing that all non-flat vectors escaping injectivity in the first half concentrate on a single universal coordinate subset $I \subseteq [n]$ of size $O(r/ζ)$, bypassing union bounds over supports; and (iii) a two-tier coordinate isolation analysis in the second half that suppresses collisions to $e^{-Ω(ζ^2)} \ll 1/r$, reliably preserving these heavy coordinates.

papers.title: Little Red Dots from Primordial Black Holes: Non-Gaussianity and Accretion Evade $μ$-Distortion Constraints
papers.authors: Shyam Balaji; Bryce Cyr; Sarah R. Geller; David I. Kaiser; Dario L. Lorenzoni et al.
papers.abstract: Recent JWST observations of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $z \gtrsim 4$ suggest the existence of early supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with masses $\gtrsim 10^6\,M_\odot$. Their rapid emergence challenges conventional seeding and growth scenarios based on accretion and mergers of Population III stellar remnants, motivating renewed interest in primordial black holes (PBHs) formed from primordial perturbations. Explaining such massive seeds requires power spectrum enhancements that are constrained by cosmic microwave background (CMB) spectral distortions. In this work we perform the first comprehensive Bayesian exploration of non-Gaussian primordial perturbations capable of producing SMBH seeds while remaining consistent with CMB spectral distortion constraints, and examine the role of accretion history in constraining these models. We perform a suite of Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses of power spectrum enhancements (lognormal and cut-power-law) with varying local non-Gaussianity and accretion histories, satisfying the COBE/FIRAS $μ$-distortion constraint with and without the requirement that the model produces SMBH seeds. We find that both models can seed LRDs and evade $μ$-distortion bounds for $|f_{\rm NL}|= O(1)$ and peak amplitude $A= O(10^{-3})$, when standard Eddington-limited accretion is also incorporated. Interestingly, the results exhibit a preference for both positive and negative values of $f_{\rm NL}$. The preference for negative $f_{\rm NL}$ is strongly dependent on the accretion history, and is removed if the black holes have a small duty cycle, $f_{\rm duty}\lesssim 0.1$. These results demonstrate that the JWST high-$z$ LRD population can be seeded by primordial perturbations while remaining compatible with CMB data, and highlight the importance of next-generation CMB spectral distortion missions to test this hypothesis.

papers.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Zheng Jiang; Fang Niu; Bo Peng; Houde Qian; Wenyi Li et al.
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

papers.title: Forward modeling linear variable filter data: High resolution PAH and Paschen-$α$ maps from SPHEREx
papers.authors: Andrew K. Saydjari; Connor Hainje; Benjamin Dodge; Philipp Frank; David W. Hogg et al.
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission is a powerful tool for the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) in both Galactic and extragalactic contexts. It can reveal ionization state, radiation field, metallicity, composition, and ISM structure as sculpted by processes like turbulence and stellar feedback. Here we use NASA's SPHEREx to produce clean, high-resolution PAH maps at spectral resolution R $\sim$ 35 (compared to WISE at R $\sim$ 2). Prior treatments of the SPHEREx linear variable filter data seek to convert them to more conventional band-averaged maps that can leave striping artifacts associated with spatially variable wavelength sampling, especially at emission lines. In contrast, we deliver a scalable forward-modeling method capable of generating high-quality all-sky SPHEREx emission-line maps at 8.5 arcsec FWHM angular resolution (on 6.4 arcsec pixels), while naturally producing maps without visible striping. We reformat the data into a pixel-level database, mask stellar contamination, and infill missing pixels with a conditional, data-driven, anisotropic Gaussian process. We apply our method to produce 3.3 $μ$m and 3.4 $μ$m PAH and Paschen-$α$ emission maps of a set of fields spanning a range of Galactic and extragalactic conditions including the Rosette nebula, the Corona Australis molecular cloud, M33, and M31. We demonstrate the quality and synergies of our SPHEREx 3.3 $μ$m PAH maps by comparisons with other available gas and dust tracer maps and achieve sensitivities up to $σ(I_{3.3}) = 2.7 \times 10^{-8}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$. We estimate that a two-year extension of the SPHEREx survey, with modest modifications to the scanning strategy, would match or exceed the PAH sensitivity of WISE over the whole sky.

papers.title: High Pressure Material Phase Identification with Gaussian Kernel Neural Networks
papers.authors: Cameron Ryan; Yasantha Pasindu Hetti Kankanamalage; Shuai Zhang
papers.abstract: Phase identification is a computational task involving the classification of material structure using the positions of atoms. Using data from Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, our task is to identify the material phase of a set of atoms, based on how the simulations predict their positioning relative to each other. By leveraging existing research on mechanistic neural network theory, particularly Neural Tangent Kernels (NTK), we develop a new and efficient method for classifying simulated material samples. Our method involves defining a set of "atom detectors" that are given positions around the origin in cartesian coordinates. The sum of Gaussians centered at each atom is calculated at each atom detector, and is used as the input to a neural network. We present theoretical and experimental evidence to show that this method is highly effective and efficient at the task. Our method obtains better or similar accuracy scores to commonly used methods while having a major computational speedup.

papers.title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
papers.authors: Aarya Bhave; Anushka Ajay Bhave
papers.abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $Φ$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

papers.title: Smartphone-Enabled Depth-Aware Transillumination Imaging for Detection of Chicken Breast Fillet Myopathies in Chicken Fillets
papers.authors: Chaitanya Pallerla; Ramesh Bahadur Bist; Yihong Feng; Yang Tian; Shiva Paudel et al.
papers.abstract: Woody Breast (WB) myopathy is a major quality defect in broiler chickens characterized by fibrosis, increased tissue hardness, and altered structural properties that affect product quality. Conventional palpation is subjective and labor-intensive, while many non-destructive methods require specialized equipment or substantial computational resources. This study developed a smartphone-based transillumination and 3D point-cloud framework for non-destructive WB severity classification. A total of 267 chicken breast fillets, including normal breast (NB, n = 87), mild WB (MWB, n = 85), and severe WB (SWB, n = 95), were evaluated using RAW transillumination images and 3D point clouds acquired with an iPhone 16 Pro. A total of 91 features, comprising 14 image-derived, 76 geometric, and one physics-informed Beer-Lambert attenuation feature, were extracted. Partial correlation controlling for thickness revealed a significant association between image characteristics and WB severity (r = 0.413, p < 0.0001), indicating optical information independent of fillet geometry. SWB tissue exhibited approximately 26% greater light attenuation per unit thickness than NB. The 2D-only models achieved approximately 82% test accuracy, while the multimodal ensemble combining Fusion-DGCNN, XGBoost, and physics-guided logistic regression (PGLR) achieved approximately 90% accuracy. These findings demonstrate the complementary value of optical, geometric, and physics-informed features and establish the feasibility of smartphone-based, non-destructive WB severity assessment.

papers.title: Brown Measures and Spectral Convergence for Arbitrary GUE Polynomials
papers.authors: Benoit Collins; Yu Kitagawa; Akihiro Miyagawa; Wangjun Yuan; Ping Zhong
papers.abstract: For arbitrary noncommutative polynomials in independent GUE matrices, we prove that the empirical eigenvalue measure converges weakly in probability to the Brown measure of the corresponding polynomial in free semicircular variables. We also prove convergence of the entire eigenvalue set in Hausdorff distance and convergence of the spectral radius, both in probability. Equivalently, these matrix conclusions hold for arbitrary $*$-polynomials in independent complex Ginibre matrices. Independently, we prove that the support of the Brown measure of every polynomial in free semicircular variables equals its operator spectrum. The proof of weak convergence combines a criterion based on the second moment of the Brown measure with complex Gaussian rotation and convexity. The support theorem uses linearization and rigidity of matrix Dyson equations.   We also prove absolute continuity for nonconstant polynomials without adjoints in free circular variables. A matrix Dyson equation recovers Brown measures of arbitrary semicircular polynomials through regularized logarithmic potentials. For drift-corrected nondegenerate elliptic free random walks, it yields quantitative convergence of potentials in the interior of the limiting domain and weak convergence of Brown measures to that of free multiplicative Brownian motion.

papers.title: Numerical Investigations on Bitumen Liberation from Oil Sands Lump
papers.authors: Mohammadhossein Golchin; Siyu Chen; Payman Esmaeili; Petr Nikrityuk; Xuehua Zhang
papers.abstract: The dynamic liberation and digestion of viscous oil-solid aggregates under turbulent flow is a critical transport phenomenon in multiphase chemical processes, including slurry transport, soil remediation, and industrial extraction. A primary industrial application of this phenomenon is oil sands hydrotransport, where pipelines are widely utilized to simultaneously transport and extract bitumen from lump ore. However, optimizing operating conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the localized hydrodynamic mechanisms governing detachment. To address this, a three-dimensional (3D) Eulerian-Eulerian (E-E) CFD approach coupled with k-omega SST turbulence model has been utilized to investigate bitumen detachment dynamics from complex solid matrices. Six numerical cases were analyzed across lump diameters (D) of 4 and 5 cm and particle Reynolds numbers (Re_p) between 2000 and 4000. The simulation results reveal that bitumen liberation is a shear-driven process, occurring only when the shear stresses exerted by the flow on the lump surface exceed a critical threshold value. The bitumen liberation rate increases with higher Re_p and smaller D, due to enhanced local shear forces and reduced particle shielding. Based on these mechanistic insights, a novel semi-empirical shear-driven model was formulated. The proposed model demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy when validated against experimental liberation data, with an error less than 8.3%. Overall, these findings clarify the fluid-particle interactions governing bitumen detachment and offer a robust, physics-based tool for predicting recovery efficiency in industrial hydrotransport operations.

papers.title: Anchor Behavior, Not Parameters: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning with a Single Shared Prompt
papers.authors: Duy-Cuong Bui; Trung-Anh Dang; Vincent Nguyen; Duc V. Le; Ngoc-Son Vu
papers.abstract: Prompt-based continual learning adapts a frozen pre-trained vision transformer by tuning a small set of prompt tokens. Recently, one-prompt methods which share one single prompt across all tasks make this paradigm maximally parameter efficient. The open question is how a shared prompt can keep the knowledge of old classes while being updated for new ones. Existing methods protect old knowledge in parameter space, where they freeze task-specific prompts, expand new components, or sparsely gate which tokens receive gradients. However, this method sacrifices plasticity, yet the drift it still permits in shared tokens can corrupt the prompt's function on past classes. What must be preserved is the prompt's behavior. We propose TEA-Prompt, which couples (i) a token evaluation module that assigns each prompt token a continuous, input-conditional relevance score injected into the attention logits, softly specializing tokens across tasks without discarding any of them, and (ii) an attention-behavior anchoring loss that constrains each token's attention output around class-specific query regions using only compact Gaussian query statistics without stored old images, weighted by the token's past relevance. Anchoring the attention value allows the parameters to continue updating freely, as long as their interaction remains unchanged. TEA-Prompt achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with markedly lower forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 with only 0.38M parameters. Code is publicy available at https://github.com/cuonga1cvp/TEA-Prompt.git

papers.title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion
papers.authors: Suryansh Talukdar; Taha Sarwat; Jin Soung Yoo
papers.abstract: Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which require GPUs at inference time and are difficult to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session using three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session's own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model, this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1-8.8M parameters and no GPU required at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 scores of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013-0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5-10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights.

papers.title: Gravitational waves and the exit from de Sitter in Inflation without an Inflaton
papers.authors: Daniele Bertacca; Raul Jimenez; Sabino Matarrese; Mariam Abdelaziz; Marisol Traforetti
papers.abstract: In Inflation without an Inflaton (IWI), second-order de Sitter (dS) gravitons generate primordial curvature as the Coulomb-type potential of their gradient stress. Each pair contributes $(p/k)^2$, yielding exponential enhancement over the contributing e-folds. With exact Bunch-Davies evolution, this solution satisfies all four scalar second-order Einstein equations in pure dS. The retarded transverse-traceless solution instead has a UV kernel of order unity, $(k/p)^2$ below the scalar kernel, and a one-loop correction $Δ^2_{h,2}/Δ^2_h\simeq0.04\,Δ^2_h$. Its source acts before internal freeze-out, but oscillatory cancellations prevent tensor enhancement.   We evolve the curvature through a smooth exit into radiation domination. Conserved curvature resides on the vacuum-decay hypersurface. A global depletion clock holds each scale on zero-shear time for $N_{\rm w}$ e-folds after horizon exit before local release, giving all scales equal enhancement. Energy-momentum conservation feeds the depleted vacuum energy into a non-vacuum sector, modeled as radiation. Deep in radiation domination, $Δ^2_ζ=c_wΔ_h^4e^{N_{\rm w}}/20$, with clock-dependent $c_w$, $n_s-1=-4ε$, and $n_T=-2ε$. The spectrum is adiabatic and Gaussian; super-horizon $ζ$ is conserved to better than $10^{-4}$, and changing the adiabatic exit fluid alters it by less than $0.2\%$. A direct radiation exit requires $31\lesssim N_{\rm w}\lesssim50$, or $3\times10^{-6}\lesssim r\lesssim0.036$.   At interferometer frequencies, $Ω_{\rm GW}h^2\simeq2\times10^{-21}$--$3\times10^{-17}$, accessible to BBO for $r\gtrsim0.01$ and ultimate DECIGO for $r\gtrsim10^{-5}$; CMB B-mode searches probe $r\gtrsim10^{-3}$. Above $k_{\rm end}e^{-N_{\rm w}}$, the scalar spectrum steepens to $k^{-1}$, suppressing $μ$-distortions for sharp release when $N_{\rm w}\gtrsim45$.

papers.title: Adaptive Output Regulation of Linear Systems with Unknown Harmonic Exosystems and Additive Noise
papers.authors: Bingsen Li; George Weiss
papers.abstract: This paper addresses error-feedback output regulation for known multivariable linear plants subject to an unknown exosystem and additive Gaussian process and measurement noise. The exosystem generates constant and sinusoidal signals, but its dimension, frequencies, and coupling matrices are unavailable. An output-injection transformation represents the external action through known channels. A causal observer then produces a residual independent of the applied input, whose filtered output separates into a harmonic signal, stationary colored Gaussian noise, and a decaying transient. Using this observation model, a Fourier procedure consistently identifies the number and values of the active positive frequencies in the presence of noise. The identified frequencies determine a regulator through interpolation with stable residual filters. A contractive filter realization, nonexpansive state resizing, and bounded gain updates ensure closed-loop moment bounds uniformly over the selected filter orders. If the gain bound contains the ideal interpolation gain, the adaptive plant response and tracking error converge in mean square to those of the corresponding known-frequency regulator. The limiting mean-square tracking error is a linear function of the process- and measurement-noise covariances. In the absence of both noises, the tracking error converges to zero.

papers.title: Transport, Entropy, and the Cost of Dependence: Maximum Conditional Entropy under Transport Constraints
papers.authors: Andre Bertolace; Konstantinos Gatsis; Kostas Margellos
papers.abstract: Maximum-entropy inference under Wasserstein constraints can be computationally challenging due to the underlying optimization over transport couplings. We investigate a tractable alternative based on maximizing conditional entropy under an average transport constraint. On Euclidean spaces, this formulation admits an explicit generalized-Gaussian additive-noise solution, providing a feasible approximation to the Wasserstein-constrained problem without solving an optimal transport problem. We establish quantitative bounds on the resulting optimality gap by showing that the two formulations admit a common feasible-marginal representation, with their discrepancy characterized by the mutual information retained between the nominal and perturbed variables. For discretely supported nominal distributions, we further obtain an exact decomposition of the gap into a marginal-entropy gain and a weighted Jensen-Shannon divergence.

papers.title: Clique Constraints for Exact Causal Structure Learning
papers.authors: Xiaoyu He; Pavel Rytíř; Petr Ryšavý; Jakub Mareček
papers.abstract: Exact score-based causal structure learning supports explicit structural constraints and optimisation certificates, but its branch-and-cut search can be computationally demanding. We augment exact causal structure learning methods with an upper bound on the maximum clique size of the learned undirected skeleton, enforced at integer candidates through lazy cycle and clique constraints. On static linear-Gaussian Erdős-Rényi and scale-free DAGs, we evaluate callback order, alternative clique-cut policies, incumbent repair, fractional separation, and Big-M bounds. We report causal-recovery metrics jointly with optimality gaps, primal and dual bounds, node throughput, MIPSOL events, and callback cost. Two variants receive particular attention: B3 selects the most violated minimal (k+1)-clique inequality at each callback, whereas C3 repairs an infeasible integer candidate by deleting violating edges and refitting affected regression columns using QR-based least squares. The results do not indicate that clique constraints uniformly accelerate optimisation. However, their benefit depends on graph density, sample size, and cut-management policy, while large collections of correlated constraints can reduce node throughput. Tighter valid Big-M bounds reduced the fixed-budget optimality gap in most tested settings, without necessarily changing SHD or F1 at a fixed time limit. These findings characterize the computational trade-offs of clique-constrained exact causal learning, and identify selective separation and incumbent repair as promising directions.

papers.title: KL-Regularized Policy Iteration for Adaptive LQR: Gain Updates and Probing from One Policy Improvement
papers.authors: Ajinkya Bhole; Mohammad Mahmoudi Filabadi; Guillaume Crevecoeur; Tom Lefebvre
papers.abstract: Policy-gradient methods for adaptive linear quadratic control improve the feedback gain of an unknown plant online by gradient-type steps computed from closed-loop data. A recent framework of such methods, policy-gradient adaptive control (PGAC), takes one gradient-type step per sample, which its indirect form computes from an estimated model and its direct form directly from the data. Because data generated by a fixed linear feedback cannot identify the plant, PGAC adds a probing perturbation to the input and leaves its covariance as a design parameter. We study the adaptive LQR problem through a KL-regularized formulation, in which the probing is the randomness of a Gaussian policy kept close to a Gaussian reference policy, so that the cost of the probing is part of the objective. One policy improvement of this formulation gives a gain update together with a probing covariance. We show that, for suitable references centred at the current gain, this gain update is exactly PGAC's Gauss-Newton or natural-gradient update with any step size below a bound. We repeat this policy improvement, each time against a tempered copy of the current policy, and refer to this scheme as KL-regularized policy iteration (KLPI). On a known plant and with tempering, the cost of KLPI's gains converges linearly to the optimal cost, and the probing covariance keeps a floor proportional to the regularization weight. On an estimated plant, under conditions like PGAC's (small updates and sufficiently informative data), the closed loop stays stable, the cost of the gains converges linearly up to a bias, and the probing covariance again keeps this floor. In simulations at equal probing cost, the shape of KLPI's probing covariance, which PGAC can adopt, lowers the extra cost caused by suboptimal gains on nearly all tested plants, whereas KLPI's use of past iterations in its gain update changes this cost little.

papers.title: Plant Orbiter: 3D Plant Reconstruction and Generation with Video Diffusion Orbit Cameras and 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Zane K. J. Hartley; Yong En Kok; Lewis A. G. Stuart; Andrew P. French; Michael P. Pound
papers.abstract: Modern digital phenotyping pipelines require the precise measurement of a range of 3D morphological plant traits. The accurate, high throughput acquisition of these traits helps breeders and researchers accelerate the development of new varieties, techniques and products. Recent advances in 3D technologies have enabled a rapid transition from 2D to 3D pipelines, but high throughput acquisition of digital 3D twins of plants remains a significant challenge due to complex morphology, thin structures and occlusions. In this paper we present Plant Orbiter, a new approach to generating 3D plants that leverages recent advances in video diffusion to produce high quality 3D Gaussian Splats of plants from a single image. We show that our method more accurately recreates plant morphology than other state-of-the-art methods, achieving the highest 3D F-score against all baselines, while being more practical for high throughput pipelines due to easier alignment and reduced cost of camera placement. Combined with a 2D diffusion model, we show that our method also achieves state-of-the-art results in the generation of 3D plant models from a text prompt.

papers.title: Out-of-plane interference effects in the angle-resolved photoemission of epitaxial graphene
papers.authors: E. Favorite; P. Krüger; Ph. Rosenzweig; R. Joshi; S. Williams et al.
papers.abstract: The epitaxial growth of monolayer graphene by Si sublimation of 6H-SiC(0001) is one of the most effective ways of producing large-scale monocrystalline graphene samples of high quality. However, graphene is left interacting with a reconstructed carbon buffer layer known as zerolayer graphene (ZLG) and the SiC substrate underneath. Beyond the mere creation of Dirac cone replicas, the effect of this interaction on photoemission measurements is poorly understood. We utilized synchrotron radiation for photon-energy-dependent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the complex final-state interactions of photoelectrons within the heterostructure of monolayer graphene, ZLG, and SiC. We identify multiple resonances in the photoemission intensity of the Dirac cone as a function of photon energy that originate from interlayer interference, confirmed with a multiple scattering model. We also demonstrate for the first time that the relative intensity of the replica bands induced by the $(6\sqrt{3} \times 6\sqrt{3})\text{R}30^\circ$ reconstruction scales with the electron kinetic energy. Finally, we resolved four nondispersing electronic states, which originate from the ZLG. Our findings show that the three-dimensional (3D) structure of SiC and ZLG manifests itself in the photoemission from two-dimensional (2D) epitaxial graphene. By revealing how 3D substrate architecture dictates the photoemission of a 2D layer, this work establishes a crucial framework for investigating the electronic structure of complex heterostructures via ARPES.

papers.title: Spaghetti Splatting: Differentiating Curvilinear Dirac Masses via Convolution
papers.authors: George Shramko; Shrisudhan Govindarajan; Rudy Lam; Yizheng Xie; Daniel Rebain et al.
papers.abstract: In production systems, 3D geometry is represented by primitives such as points, lines, and triangles, as rendering hardware is optimized to generate images from them very efficiently. Learning such primitives from images by volume rendering is challenging, as they are Dirac masses defined at infinitesimal locations in space. EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction, and 3D Gaussian Splatting overcome this by convolving Dirac masses with a low-frequency kernel, a recipe that generalizes along two axes: the kernel and the primitive. As points and triangles have already received significant attention, we investigate this recipe for curvilinear primitives, and introduce Spaghetti Splatting. We approximate curves by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve, and volume render each segment so that connected segments composite without overcounting at their joints. For fast training and inference, we linearize the camera projection per segment, which also accommodates kernels beyond Gaussians, such as Beta kernels. As a point is a curve of zero length, our representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It remains competitive with the state-of-the-art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands that are directly amenable to physics simulation.

papers.title: TACTUS: A Robotic Palpation System for Spatially Heterogeneous Hardness Mapping of Woody Breast Myopathy
papers.authors: Chaitanya Pallerla; Yihong Feng; Avisekh Tripathy; Yang Tian; Pouya Sohrabipour et al.
papers.abstract: Woody breast (WB) myopathy is a spatially heterogeneous fibro-degenerative condition of the broiler Pectoralis major muscle. Existing mechanical reference methods rely on single-point or sequential compression measurements, limiting characterization of spatial hardness variability. This study presents TACTUS (Tactile Adaptive Conformal 3D Uniform Sensing), an automated tactile array that generates thickness-normalized, three-dimensional hardness maps at 20 anatomically distributed locations within approximately 30 s. TACTUS integrates 20 independently motorized tactuators with force-sensing resistors and encoder-driven linear actuators, alongside a LiDAR depth camera for surface profiling and adaptive compression. The system was evaluated using 100 broiler breast fillets across four WB severity classes (Normal, Mild, Moderate, Severe). TACTUS identified significant force differences among severity classes (ANOVA, p < 0.001), with the strongest differentiation in the cranial region and a significant caudal effect not detected by texture-analyzer measurements. Fillet-level TACTUS force showed moderate but significant correlation with texture-analyzer measurements (Pearson r = 0.441, p < 0.001). Semivariogram, local change entropy, and heterogeneity analyses revealed increasing and anatomically structured hardness variability with WB severity. These findings demonstrate TACTUS as an automated, operator-independent platform for spatially resolved mechanical characterization and ground-truth generation to support hyperspectral and near-infrared spectroscopy-based WB classification systems.

papers.title: A four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: a body composition case study
papers.authors: Mariela Talavera-Muñoz; Cecilia Diana-Albelda; Miguel Antonio Sampedro-Nuñez; Victor Rodriguez-Laval; Jesus Bescos et al.
papers.abstract: Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET) lack prognostic biomarkers, and computed tomography (CT)-based body composition radiomics at the third lumbar vertebra (L3) is a promising candidate. Small cohorts make high-dimensional radiomic models prone to overfitting and single-split evaluations variable and optimistic.   This methodological study proposes a four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: (1) false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected feature selection, (2) a dual-path comparison of prior feature selection versus embedded regularization, (3) repeated nested cross-validation (CV) and (4) a negative control with Gaussian noise features. In 78 GEP-NET patients, 535 radiomic features from five L3 compartments were used to evaluate five survival models with Harrell's concordance index (C-index), time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and integrated Brier score (IBS).   Step 1 selected at least one feature in 18% of outer folds under noise (nominal level 20%) versus 84% with radiomic features. The dual-path comparison showed no consistent difference between strategies. Repeated nested CV reduced variability across seeds (41% median reduction in C-index standard deviation), but not enough to distinguish models. The nested CV C-index exceeded chance by 0.07-0.15 with radiomic features but not clearly under noise (0.40-0.42 with prior feature selection, 0.47-0.55 with embedded regularization). Frequently selected features tentatively linked greater subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle compactness and texture to better prognosis.   These findings suggest a modest prognostic signal in L3 radiomics, with considerable uncertainty that the protocol quantifies. The protocol may transfer to other small-cohort radiomic survival studies. Code: https://github.com/marielatalaveram/radiomics-survival-validation-protocol.

papers.title: Global zero distribution and pluripolar exceptional cones for complex linear differential equations
papers.authors: Xing-Yu Li
papers.abstract: We study the zeros of solutions of complex linear differential equations of arbitrary order $n\ge2$ with exponential-sum coefficients. Using the initial-value space $\mathbb{C}^n$ to parametrize the solutions, we show that solutions with initial vectors outside a complete pluripolar cone of Lebesgue measure zero share an explicit common leading term for the global zero count and a common joint limit in radius and angle. The rescaled radial distance from the disk boundary has an exponential limiting distribution, while the rescaled angular deviations from each main ray are Gaussian. Inspired by logarithmic tracts in the Eremenko-Lyubich class $\mathcal{B}$, we pull exterior sectors back conformally to countably many curvilinear strips extending in finitely many directions and obtain zero-counting asymptotics in each strip, although the coefficients may lie outside this class. Moreover, the asymptotic formula for the global zero count and the joint limit in radius and angle persist under arbitrary entire perturbations of strictly smaller weighted exponential type.

papers.title: Ground-state phase diagram of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg zigzag ladder with anisotropic $Γ$ term revisited
papers.authors: Toshiya Hikihara; Nobuya Maeshima; Kouichi Okunishi
papers.abstract: We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet with an anisotropic $Γ$ term on a zigzag ladder, which can be exactly mapped to the spin-1/2 XYZ zigzag ladder by a spin rotation. This model has recently attracted considerable interest as an effective model for the quasi-one-dimensional magnetic semiconductor YbCuS$_2$. For the model, the ground-state phase diagram was previously proposed by Saito and Hotta [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 166701 (2024); Phys. Rev. B 110, 024409 (2024)]. We systematically reexamine the phase diagram through complementary numerical and analytical approaches, including exact diagonalization, the density-matrix renormalization group method, and low-energy effective theories. We thereby demonstrate that when the anisotropic $Γ$ term is present, the model exhibits the Néel, dimer, ferromagnetic, and double-Néel phases, all of which have a finite excitation gap. The gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger-liquid (TLL) phase appears only in the isotropic case where the $Γ$ term is absent. We also confirm that the transitions between the Néel and dimer phases and between the Néel and ferromagnetic phases are continuous transitions governed by Gaussian criticality with central charge $c=1$. The TLL parameter characterizing the critical states at the Gaussian transitions is estimated numerically.

papers.title: Maurer-Inspired Two-Way Physical-Layer Authentication Against Multi-Antenna Impersonation Attacks
papers.authors: Pin-Hsun Lin; Linda Senigagliesi; Eduard A. Jorswieck
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate Maurer-inspired two-way physical-layer authentication. Alice seeks authentication by Bob in the presence of a multi-antenna impersonator, Trudy. Trudy may replace the challenge to Alice, the response to Bob, or both. To create an information advantage, Bob adds artificial noise (AN) to his challenge, and Alice adds spatial AN while forwarding the received mixture. Bob predicts the response from trusted preparation, whereas Trudy observes only a noisy version of the challenge, and Alice's AN interferes with Trudy's preparation reception. Impersonation thus requires matching Bob's fresh randomness beyond the channel consistency checked by public-pilot one-way authentication. For quasi-static Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output channels with time-division duplex (TDD) reciprocity, we derive missed-detection bounds for attacks that replace the authentication challenge, the response, or both. These bounds assume attack-free initial training and preparation and account for estimation error and AN leakage. With equal antenna numbers at all nodes, we show scenarios where the proposed scheme has lower worst-case missed detection than specified one-way tests with/without AN.

papers.title: Three-dimensional radiative transfer modeling of the scattering polarization in the solar H$α$ line
papers.authors: Jaume Jaume Bestard; Jiri Stepan; Javier Trujillo Bueno
papers.abstract: The H$α$ line probes the solar chromosphere, but its scattering polarization is difficult to interpret because of magnetic fields, plasma motions, and atmospheric 3D inhomogeneities. We investigate its intensity and linear polarization in a 3D magnetohydrodynamic solar-atmosphere model including nonequilibrium hydrogen ionization. Using PORTA, we solve the full 3D non-LTE polarized radiative transfer problem for a multilevel hydrogen atom, accounting for atomic polarization, Hanle depolarization, horizontal radiative transfer, and macroscopic velocities. We degrade synthetic Stokes profiles to the spatial, spectral, and polarimetric resolution of ZIMPOL observations for direct comparison. The modeled center-to-limb variation follows the observed trend, with comparable polarization amplitudes. The profiles show large spatial variability from symmetry breaking by horizontal inhomogeneities and atmospheric dynamics, as well as diverse line-core asymmetries. Classifying $Q/I$ profiles by asymmetry reveals a statistical correlation between profile morphology and magnetic-field strength in the H$α$ formation region, consistent with Hanle depolarization: multi-peaked profiles favor stronger fields, whereas asymmetric single-peaked profiles favor weaker fields with smaller vertical strength variations. Thus, H$α$ scattering polarization reflects the interplay of magnetic fields, velocity gradients, and 3D radiative transfer. Our results highlight the need for 3D modeling to interpret H$α$ spectropolarimetry and its potential to diagnose chromospheric magnetism and dynamics.

papers.title: Diophantine conditions for absolute continuity of projections for self-similar measures
papers.authors: Xiong Jin; Tuomas Sahlsten
papers.abstract: We prove that every projection of a planar self-similar measure $μ$ is equivalent to Lebesgue measure on its support if the rotations satisfy a simultaneous Diophantine condition with exponent $τ$ and $μ$ has finite $s$-energy for some $1+2τ\le s<2$. Under strong separation, we prove the fibre measures have exact dimension $\dim_Hμ-1$. For self-similar sets $E$ with $\dim_H E>1+2τ$, the same rotation condition implies uniformly positive projection lengths and fibres of dimension $\dim_H E-1$ at Lebesgue-almost every point of each image without separation assumptions. The absolute continuity and fibre dimension theorems extend to non-coordinate projections of products under a joint Diophantine condition with exponent $τ$ on the logarithmic contraction ratios. These imply for all self-similar sets $K,L\subset\mathbb R$ satisfying this condition and $\dim_HK+\dim_HL>1+2τ$, every sum $uK+L$, $u\ne 0$, has positive length, and $\dim_H(L\cap(y-uK))=\dim_HK+\dim_HL-1$ for Leb. a.e. $y\in uK+L$. The proof combines the $L^1$ Gaussian smoothing approach used in the higher dimensional case with averaging at random stopping scales with a Brownian martingale bound using Itô calculus.

papers.title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
papers.authors: Madhav R. Muthyala; Mahsa Askari; Farshud Sorourifar; Evan Zhou; Joe Gauthier et al.
papers.abstract: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

papers.title: Resolving the backbone of multiscale interactions through mutual information rates
papers.authors: Alberto Raiola; Giorgio Nicoletti; Daniel Maria Busiello
papers.abstract: Natural systems are often composed of processes evolving on multiple timescales and coupled through complex interaction networks. Inferring such networks is especially challenging when timescales are widely separated, since resolving the fastest processes while accurately sampling the slowest ones is generally prohibitive. In this work, we propose a framework to reconstruct a multiscale interaction tree by combining a rescaled version of the mutual information rate, its conditional counterpart, and the ordering of timescales. We derive an exact theory for stationary Gaussian processes, finding that these measures identify directly connected processes, with the asymptotic mutual information rate distinguishing fast-to-slow from slow-to-fast couplings. We show that this reconstruction can be achieved from the spectral matrix and illustrate its robustness to finite trajectory lengths, moderate timescale separation, and weak nonlinearities. Our work paves the way for exploiting the presence of multiple timescales in real-world systems as a source of structural identifiability rather than an obstacle to network inference.

papers.title: Kinematic Signatures of Stellar Flybys in Protoplanetary Discs
papers.authors: Vasundhara R. Prasad; Cristiano Longarini; Carolin N. Kimmig; Cathie J. Clarke
papers.abstract: Recent high-resolution molecular line observations of protoplanetary discs have revealed large-scale non-Keplerian features in the gas kinematics of several systems, which can be interpreted as signatures of warps in the disc. Warps can arise from a range of physical mechanisms, and it remains unclear whether the observed kinematic residuals can be uniquely attributed to warping, or to different competing effects. Stellar flybys are one such mechanism capable of both warping a disc and directly perturbing its kinematics. Using 3D smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations, we study the evolution of protoplanetary discs perturbed by inclined and coplanar stellar flybys, focusing on timescales of several thousand years after periastron rather than the immediate aftermath of the encounter. We find that inclined stellar flybys initially induce warping and twisting in the disc, but that this geometric perturbation is damped on a timescale set by the disc viscosity. Despite this geometric damping, synthetic ALMA observations of the CO kinematics show that complex non-Keplerian spiral features persist in the velocity residuals long after the warped morphology has relaxed, including in coplanar encounters where no warp is ever induced. Fitting these residuals with a simple warped-disc model, the degree of warping in the disc is systematically overestimated. We therefore conclude that kinematic residuals alone are insufficient to establish that a disc is warped, as flybys induce kinematic complexity independently of warps. We further show that scattered light observations provide an independent diagnostic, showing spiral arms and lateral asymmetries.

papers.title: Entropy: the Route from the Gaussian Field to the Statistical Mechanics of the Thermal Radiation
papers.authors: Arnaldo Spalvieri
papers.abstract: Maximum Entropy or canonical typicality applied to the electromagnetic field can provide starting points for arriving at the Bose distribution of the photon numbers of thermal radiation, but they rely on statistical postulates whose experimental testability is controversial.   Here we start from experimentally verifiable assumption of Gaussianity of the electromagnetic field. We analyze the field by projecting it onto orthonormal time-frequency basis functions with unitary bandwidth duration product that represent field's orthogonal time-frequency modes. Through the Glauber-Surashdan representation, we see that the joint density operator of the modes in the photon number basis factorize into diagonal density operators with geometric coefficients of individual modes, while the mean photon occupations of the modes remains still unknown. The independent imposition of Clausius' relation on each one of the entropies and energies of the modes leads to Bose's mean photon occupancy.   Thus, our main claim is that for the first time Bose statistics is recovered in the paper under explicit, experimentally verifiable statistical assumptions, without assuming any statistical postulate that is not directly experimentally verifiable.   From the mean occupation numbers, the Boltzmann distribution of the energy of matter particles of the material that generates/absorbes the radiation is then derived by retracing in the backward direction the Einstein-Feynman detailed balance.

papers.title: EditJudge-Bench: Auditing VLM Image-Edit Judges with Synthetic Ground Truth
papers.authors: Jens Parslov; Marco Schouten; Dim P. Papadopoulos
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for image-editing benchmarks, yet their reliability is poorly understood. Auditing these judges is difficult because real edited images lack controlled ground truth and entangle the requested changes with model artefacts, unintended side effects, and ambiguous degrees of success. In this paper, we introduce EditJudge-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,382 synthetic before/after image pairs rendered in Blender, with edits parameterised across nine categories derived from real user requests and exact ground truth from known 3D scene parameters. Because every edit is generated by a known intervention on a controlled scene, EditJudge-Bench evaluates VLM judges as binary verifiers of whether an instruction was correctly executed, isolating judge perception from editor quality. Across 25 judge configurations, we find substantial reliability gaps: (a) the widely adopted VIEScore template reaches only 69.0% AUROC with GPT-4o; (b) fine-tuned judges score 51.7-66.3%; spatial edits such as rotation and shape remain challenging; (c) prompt-formatting choices like image-text ordering shift performance by up to 14.1 points. Despite using only synthetic data, judge rankings on EditJudge-Bench correlate strongly with two real-image human-preference benchmarks ($ρ$=0.95 and $ρ$=0.71), indicating that controlled audits surface failure modes relevant to real evaluation.

papers.title: MARS: Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams for Video Forgery Detection
papers.authors: Ahmed Y. Radwan; Shaina Raza
papers.abstract: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars

papers.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
papers.authors: Klemens Flöge; Simon Bing; Leo Grinsztajn; Eliott Kalfon; Lennart Purucker et al.
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

papers.title: Revealing laser-induced modification of weak ferromagnetism through a spin-reorientation phase transition in iron borate Fe$_3$BO$_6$
papers.authors: A. V. Kuzikova; S. N. Barilo; R. A. Lanovsky; A. V. Sadovnikov; R. V. Pisarev et al.
papers.abstract: In the iron oxide Fe$_3$BO$_6$ weak ferromagnetism stems from competing contributions from two-site Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) and from on-site anisotropies at the two $4c$ and $8d$ types of nonequivalent Fe$^{3+}$ sites. As a result, spin reorientation (SR) transition $Γ_2$ $\rightarrow$ $Γ_4$ in Fe$_3$BO$_6$ uniquely comprises 90$^\circ$ spin switching and a 35% change of weak ferromagnetic moment. We explore ultrafast kinetics of such a transition as a proxy for weak ferromagnetism contributions modified by femtosecond laser pulses. Using magneto-optical pump-probe technique we reveal that the SR transition is triggered by an abrupt decrease of the weak ferromagnetic moment in the $Γ_2$ phase, and relate it to the laser-induced modification of the DMI and anisotropy contributions to the spin canting. By tuning the pump pulse phonon energy between different optical absorption ranges, we show that laser-driven impact on spin canting possesses a nonthermal character and is achieved through the charge-transfer transitions $2p\rightarrow3d$ within Fe$^{3+}$O$^{2-}_6$ octahedra rather than by localized $3d\rightarrow3d$ transitions at Fe$^{3+}$. The decreased weak ferromagnetic moment controls the threshold and the latency of the SR transition, as well as a final state. The latter is achieved via the precessional switching to the $Γ_4$ phase activated by the laser-induced heating. Final state is found to be a coexistence of $Γ_4$ and $Γ_2$ phase with modified spin canting persisting even at hundreds of picoseconds.

papers.title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
papers.authors: Roger Guimerà; Kai-Hendrik Cohrs; Sergio Pedreira; Marta Sales-Pardo; Gustau Camps-Valls
papers.abstract: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

papers.title: The symmetric Gaussian isoperimetric problem in the plane
papers.authors: Emanuel Milman
papers.abstract: We resolve the symmetric Gaussian isoperimetric conjecture in the plane: every minimizer of Gaussian perimeter among centrally symmetric sets of prescribed Gaussian measure is a centered ball, a symmetric strip, or the complement of one of these sets. A quadrant-reflection argument reduces the problem to unconditional sets. The planar structural results of Barchiesi, Cagnetti and Julin then leave only a noncircular strictly convex stationary oval. We exclude this oval by an explicit volume-preserving and perimeter-decreasing linear deformation, which geometrically corresponds to an "unconditional squeezing". More generally, without requiring any symmetry assumptions, we show that any noncircular closed embedded $λ$-self-shrinker is always unstable via linear deformations. We also record a reduction to the unconditional case in dimension three, using an orthogonal equipartition theorem of Musin.

papers.title: V3DSAM: Semantic-Geometric Loop Verification and Geometry-Anchored Persistent Instance Mapping for Feed-Forward Dense SLAM
papers.authors: Maolin Ye; Dongqing Zhao; Linyang Li; Shuai Xue; Yuan Liu et al.
papers.abstract: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.

papers.title: Sensitivity of diffusion MRI to white matter pathology: a comparison between ROI-based effect size and TBSS analysis under different diffusion protocols, field strengths and post-processing strategies
papers.authors: Evgenios N. Kornaropoulos; Theodor Rumetshofer; Anna Gard; Linda Knutsson; Niklas Marklund et al.
papers.abstract: We investigated how much more advanced diffusion MRI acquisitions and more complex processing increase sensitivity to group-wise white matter (WM) differences due to pathology, and how the choice of statistical analysis affects this sensitivity. Data were acquired with DTI and DKI protocols at 3T and 7T in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS), and healthy controls (HC). Seven processing pipelines combining denoising, Gibbs removal, eddy current and motion correction, and Gaussian smoothing were applied. Sensitivity was assessed with two methods: a region-of-interest-based (ROI-based) effect size analysis over 72 WM tracts segmented by TractSeg, quantified by Cohen's d, and tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS), quantified by the fraction of significant voxels in the WM skeleton. The ROI-based analysis found significant group differences for both SLE versus HC and PPCS versus HC, whereas TBSS found differences only for SLE versus HC. Both analyses agreed that the diffusion protocol affected sensitivity more than field strength or post-processing. Regardless of pipeline, DTI-derived fractional anisotropy (FA) yielded a 0.26 higher effect size and 25% more significantly different voxels between SLE and HC than DKI-derived FA, and 3T yielded a 0.2 higher effect size and 21% more significant voxels than 7T. Smoothing reduced sensitivity in both analyses (by up to 12% in TBSS for SLE versus HC). Overall, TBSS appears less suited to localized pathology such as neurotrauma, whereas the ROI-based analysis showed no bias with respect to the nature of the pathology. Advanced protocols such as 3T-DKI and 7T-DTI may need further optimization before surpassing conventional 3T-DTI in sensitivity to WM pathology in SLE.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks in the small-data regime: A controlled comparison with classical PDE surrogates
papers.authors: Kirill Katsuba; Oleg Rudenko; Egor Bugaev; Alexander Tarakanov
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for engineering models are often trained on large collections of simulated solutions. We investigate whether physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can achieve accurate predictions from scarce labelled observations by incorporating governing equations and prescribed initial and boundary conditions. We introduce hierarchical loss weighting (H-PINN) and its gradient-direction-aware extension (HO-PINN), which adjust the emphasis on physical constraints according to higher-priority losses. Hierarchical PINNs are compared with Vanilla PINN, tuned gradient boosting, support-vector regression, and Gaussian-process regression on a heat equation and three heterogeneous two-phase-flow benchmarks. Experiments use 20--1000 labelled states and ten paired seeds. Each label is one coordinate--state observation, not a complete simulation. At least one PINN variant achieves the highest mean primary-target \(R^2\) in each interpolation and equation-assisted forecasting comparison at 20 and 50 labels. The advantage for water saturation persists across all tested budgets. Hierarchical weighting reduces variability across runs in selected settings. These results demonstrate that known physics can support accurate neural surrogate predictions from very few solution observations, at substantially higher fitting cost than the tested classical regressors.

papers.title: Optimal Rates for Adaptive Private $k$-PCA
papers.authors: Johanna Düngler; Amartya Sanyal
papers.abstract: Given $n$ i.i.d. random matrices $A_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ with common expectation $Σ$, the goal of \emph{Differentially Private Stochastic PCA} is to identify a $k$-dimensional subspace capturing the leading variance directions of $Σ$, while preserving differential privacy~(DP) for each individual sample $A_i$. \citet{dungler2025iterative} introduced \kdppca, the first algorithm to simultaneously (1) achieve sample complexity $n=\widetilde O(d)$ for sub-Gaussian data, (2) adapt its privacy noise to the intrinsic randomness of the data, and (3) extend seamlessly to any target dimension $k\le d$. However, its sample complexity has a suboptimal dependence on $k$. We propose the first algorithm that achieves optimal sample complexity in both $d$ and $k$, while retaining properties (2) and (3) of \kdppca. Additionally, prior utility guarantees require a minimum sample size with exponential dependence on the eigengap. Our method removes this dependence. It also improves the dependence on spectral parameters, matching known lower bounds for the spiked covariance model. Unlike deflation-based approaches like \kdppca, our algorithm updates the full $d\times k$ subspace jointly rather than one eigenvector at a time. This non-deflation structure simplifies the algorithm, reduces the number of hyper-parameters, and improves computational efficiency, particularly when using block linear algebra libraries.

papers.title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation
papers.authors: Manas Sharma; Marek Sierka
papers.abstract: We present a direct-space formulation and implementation of quantum density functional theory (DFT) embedding for molecular active subsystems embedded in frozen environments (hosts) of arbitrary dimensionality, from finite molecular hosts to extended systems. The host is computed once without the embedded molecule (the guest) and is represented only by its electron density fitted in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian basis together with its nuclear charges with the periodic electrostatics separated into an explicit near-field and a continuous fast-multipole far-field operator. The method allows the removal of host atoms from this representation to create vacancies or other voids without requiring a supercell creation. Analytic nuclear gradients are also implemented, enabling structural relaxation of the active subsystem. We demonstrate the versatility of the approach through applications to adsorbates on periodic surfaces and molecules embedded in bulk solvent environments. For CO on MgO(001), we show that DFT-in-DFT converges rapidly and reproduces the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol while reducing the cost by a factor of 27. Real-time time-dependent embedded DFT (RT-TDDFET) of methylenecyclopropene in periodic water is showcased to produce a ~0.6 eV solvatochromic blue shift, while strong-field propagation of CO2 on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) yields substrate-induced effects at the cost of a gas-phase propagation. Coupling the embedding scheme to excited-state correlated wave function theory methods such as CC2 yields a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 references, while reducing the computational cost by over 500 times.

papers.title: Evidence or Marginal? What Moment-Vector Propagation Computes in Polynomial Density Neurons
papers.authors: Przemysław Spyra
papers.abstract: When a neuron's input is lost, or known through a belief $q$, what should it output? For a neuron storing a joint polynomial density $N$ with input density $D$, two formulas compete. $p_\mathrm{CD}=E_q[N]/E_q[D]$ costs one matrix-vector product; Hierarchical Correlation Reconstruction introduces it as a constant-denominator approximation to $p_\mathrm{EU}=E_q[N/D]$. For a density model both are exact answers to different questions: $p_\mathrm{CD}$ is Bayesian updating with the belief as virtual evidence; $p_\mathrm{EU}$ installs the belief as a new marginal (Jeffrey's rule). With a missing input $p_\mathrm{CD}$ returns the model's conditional; $p_\mathrm{EU}$ generally does not. This post hoc reading is proved, and illustrated outside the pair family up to $k=8$ inputs; it has no pre-registered test, only one exploratory real-data pilot. Post hoc, closed forms fall within a factor 2 of all 112 measured gaps, and negative density begins near input correlation $1/k$. In a pre-registered synthetic study (up to 32 inputs), 5 of 15 hypotheses are supported, 2 inconclusive and 8 not supported, including all three on transfer beyond equicorrelated Gaussians. Post hoc, where $p_\mathrm{EU}$ is defined, truncation usually outweighs the gap for Beta beliefs in pair neurons; triple neurons under flat and data beliefs are exceptions.

papers.title: Rethinking Radar 3D Perception: Representation Learning from Raw Spectra
papers.authors: Miao Zhang; Mohamed Abdelsamad; Bin Yang; Sherif Abdulatif; Benedikt Loesch et al.
papers.abstract: Raw radar spectra are widely viewed as too cluttered and noisy for direct representation learning, motivating handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds, or compact Doppler descriptors in radar perception. We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.

papers.title: SimpFlow: Transferable Pretraining for Fluid Dynamics via Simplified Physics
papers.authors: Ruijie Li; Tianbai Xiao
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates enable rapid fluid simulation, but learning across diverse three-dimensional (3D) geometries requires costly computational fluid dynamics (CFD) labels. We introduce SimpFlow, a pretraining approach that generates supervision from simplified physics on unlabeled geometry libraries. A source-panel potential-flow solver generates velocity and pressure fields for approximately 9,000 3D geometries, capturing geometry-induced acceleration, stagnation, and suction while omitting viscosity and separated wakes. The solver imports only a surface mesh and reuses precomputed velocity fields across inflow directions, enabling inexpensive label generation. In our benchmark, amortized labeling takes 0.111 s per example using four CPU threads. We pretrain a neural surrogate on these labels and fine-tune it on independent CFD datasets. Across five flow tasks, SimpFlow improves over training from scratch in all 24 task-budget settings. With fine-tuning fixed at 200 epochs, interpolation indicates that SimpFlow requires 35-68% fewer CFD training cases to match the error of scratch models trained at each task's largest data budget. These results demonstrate that simplified physical solutions can provide transferable supervision, offering a practical way to reduce the high-fidelity data requirements of fluid surrogates.

papers.title: Data-Adaptive Subset-Size Selection for Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimation
papers.authors: Chikun Li; Baisuo Jin
